title: Ruthless prioritization: 10x / 0.1x tasks and explaining why the dog pees on the floor
summary: Time is zero-sum and you can do maybe 1-10% of what you "need" to, so Jason Cohen proposes a binary 10x / 0.1x framework: hunt for the few transformative tasks, and delegate, batch, automate or archive the rest. Then keep explaining the "not doing" list so the team doesn't lose faith while some fires burn on purpose.

principles.text: Time lets you do only 1-10% of what you need to, so prioritization is mandatory.
principles.quote: So, time is a fixed constraint that limits us to 1%-10% of what we "need" to execute. Unintuitively, the fraction diminishes with scale; we will never defeat it.

principles.text: If you can't name your one or two 10x tasks, finding them is your top priority.
principles.quote: If you don't know what one or two 10x tasks you should be working on, then *identifying that is your highest priority*.

principles.text: A true 10x bet must survive running 2x longer and delivering half the impact.
principles.quote: Their upside must be so massive, that even when it inevitably takes 2x longer to implement and is $\frac{1}{2}$ as impactful as you thought, it was still worth it.

principles.text: Minimize 0.1x work: eliminate it by design, delegate even if worse, batch or automate, and archive old tickets.
principles.quote: Archive loose tickets that are older than 100 days. Because of the rule that more than 90% of our ideas will never be done, realize that these are already among that 90%

principles.text: Easy is not the same as low impact; don't conflate effort with impact when sorting tasks.
principles.quote: It's tempting to assume that small, easy tasks are automatically 0.1x tasks, but that is a fallacy of conflating "impact" with "effort".

principles.text: Ruthless prioritization leaves real fires burning; keep telling the full story and the "not doing" list or the team loses trust.
principles.quote: You have to acknowledge the twenty things other that also deserve attention, explaining why we're intentionally letting those fires burn, those dogs pee, because the top priorities are even more important.
